explanation:
## 262,144 lines

The bound is a counting argument and does not mention the loop at all:

```
elements per matrix     = n^2            = 1,048,576
bytes per matrix        = n^2 x 8        = 8 MiB
doubles per 64B line    = 8
lines per matrix        = n^2 / 8        = 131,072
both matrices           = 2 x n^2 / 8    = n^2 / 4 = 262,144
```

Every element of `a` must be read and every element of `b` must be written. Memory moves in lines. In the best case each line of each matrix is transferred exactly once, which gives `n^2/4` and cannot be beaten.

## What the naive loop actually does

```c
b[j][i] = a[i][j];      /* i outer, j inner */
```

- **Reading `a[i][j]`** walks contiguously along a row. One miss brings in eight doubles and the next seven accesses hit. Cost: `n^2/8` = 131,072 lines. Optimal.
- **Writing `b[j][i]`** strides down a column — consecutive writes are `n x 8 = 8192` bytes apart. Every single write touches a different line, and by the time the loop returns to a neighbouring element, that line has long been evicted. Cost: `n^2` = 1,048,576 lines. **Eight times optimal.**

```
naive total  = n^2 + n^2/8 = 9n^2/8 = 1,179,648
optimal      =              n^2/4   =   262,144
ratio        = 4.5x
```

So the naive transpose moves four and a half times the minimum traffic. On a memory-bound operation — and a transpose does no arithmetic at all, so it is as memory-bound as anything gets — that is very nearly four and a half times the runtime.

Note that swapping the loops does not help. It makes the write contiguous and the read strided, and the total is the same `9n^2/8`. The problem is not which loop is outer; it is that one of the two arrays must be strided if you traverse either in order.

## How tiling reaches the bound

Work on an 8x8 block at a time — eight doubles is exactly one line:

```c
const int B = 8;
for (int ii = 0; ii < n; ii += B)
    for (int jj = 0; jj < n; jj += B)
        for (int i = ii; i < ii + B; i++)
            for (int j = jj; j < jj + B; j++)
                b[j][i] = a[i][j];
```

Per tile: 8 lines of `a` (one per row of the tile) and 8 lines of `b`. Both tiles stay resident while the 64 assignments happen, so each line is touched once and then finished with.

```
tiles        = (n/8)^2 = 16,384
lines / tile = 16
total        = 262,144      <- exactly the bound
```

**The flop count is identical. The traffic is 4.5x lower.** No arithmetic was removed, no instruction was made faster; the only change is the order in which memory is touched. That is the whole argument for tiling, and it is why it matters far more than micro-optimising the loop body on anything memory-bound.

## Why 8 and not 64

Two forces pull in opposite directions. The tile must be big enough that a line is fully used — `B >= 8` for doubles in 64-byte lines. It must be small enough that `2 x B^2` doubles fit comfortably in L1, and that the `B` lines of `b` do not collide in a set-associative cache. For a 32 KiB 8-way L1, `B` of 8 to 32 is the usual sweet spot, and it is worth measuring rather than deriving: the cache is set-associative, and a tile whose rows are a power-of-two stride apart can map every row to the same set and thrash despite fitting on paper. Padding the row stride by one line is the standard trick, and it looks like a waste of memory until you measure it.

## The version that needs no tile size

A **cache-oblivious** transpose recurses — split the matrix in half along its longer dimension and transpose each half — until the pieces are small. It reaches the same `O(n^2/L)` bound for *every* level of the cache hierarchy at once, with no tile size to tune and no knowledge of the line size. Frigo et al.'s paper is the one to read, and the idea is genuinely surprising the first time: you can be optimal at every cache level simultaneously without knowing anything about any of them.
